notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00544.opp-gr: §5: the text after κινδυνεύω appears lacunose (the contrast between the speaker's danger and the city's is incomplete; αὑτήν presumably refers to the city); rendered literally with [...]. §6: 'ἐμὲ γὰρ ὁ οὐ μικρὸς' is corrupt or lacunose (a noun such as 'uproar' seems lost, and a verb like 'chose' is missing). §8: ἀκεδέχασθε read as ἀπεδέξασθε; οὗς as οὖν. Other evident scanning errors (ρυλακήν, ιύκ, δίον = δέον, ποιεῖω, παλεμίους) silently corrected.
18: the opening 'this very thing' refers to the proof by testimony just described. 23: taxiarchs and phylarchs are infantry and cavalry commanders.

36: 'προκυλινδεῖσθαι εἷσθαι' read as a dittography; translated as προκυλινδεῖσθαι. 39: the subject of 'would gladly have borne' is unclear; taken as the deserters' own side. 45: stray '15' (a printed line number) omitted. 48: 'τοὺς ... πεπονηκότα' read as τὸν ... πεπονηκότα.

In 71 ἀπίωσιν 'depart' is taken as departing life (being put to death). In 74 ἔμεν read as ἴμεν 'we are going'; 'carried out' renders ἐξενεχθήσεται (divulged abroad). In 78 a stray bracket after ἡμεῖς is omitted; λοχαγοί rendered 'captains'. In 80 πρὸς ὕδωρ ἀγῶνας taken as trials timed by the water-clock, i.e. regular courts. 'This man' in 80 presumably refers to the accuser.

nodes.text: XLIV.

A law [provides] that a foreigner seen in the assembly is to be put to death by the general. A foreigner was seen, and as he was being led away he said that he had a secret to reveal. The general killed him. After this the city fell under a tyranny. When the tyrant has been overthrown, [the general] is tried as an accomplice.
The declamation.

The evils that come from tyranny, gentlemen, and that it is the harshest of all the terrible things among men, the accuser seems to me to have shown well enough, and to have made his speech equal to the disasters. But that I helped to prepare any of this against you, and that I wanted a master set over the city, this, by the gods, he seemed to me unable to show by any argument at all.

If you make the nature of what happened a charge against me, and think you ought to exact from those who have done you no wrong the penalty for what you suffered at the tyrant's hands, do whatever you wish. But if what you suffered from him is one thing, and my having been wicked towards the city is another, do not stand by and let me be destroyed by speeches against tyranny, and do not let loose your anger at it upon one of those whom you have trusted.

I seem to be the most unfortunate man in the city, if every other man is cheerful, wears a garland and enjoys the change in affairs, while I alone both experienced the hardships of the tyranny and am deprived of the blessings of freedom.

And it seems to me that those who loudly claim to love democracy and to make war on tyranny are increasing the hardships of tyranny and opposing the blessings that come from freedom. For to harass any citizen one happens upon and to seek to kill him on false charges by the vote of deceived jurors is as much more terrible than suffering such a thing by command as the one happens because of the times, and it is usual for a slave to endure some injustice, whereas, among those who are thought to be strong in laws and in the form of a democracy, to be put to death contrary to the laws is a greater misfortune for the one who dies and a disgrace to those who vote, if under freedom some suffer and others imitate the acts of tyranny. So if you care that the constitution be restored in purity, listen also to the defendant's speech with goodwill.

5. I think I shall not be wrong in saying that I am in danger [...] about whether [the city] ought to seem sensible; for generalship is not at the disposal of whoever wants it, but whomever you choose, having judged him fit to manage the greatest of your affairs, he is appointed master of the forces. If, when I present what is just, your [verdict] does not go against it, the defendant will have safety, and the city will gain good repute from entrusting its management to good men; but if you prefer the slanders of the informers to a correct defence, I shall die, and you will be thought to outdo everyone in folly, if those whom you were going to put to death as most wicked were the men you were leading to the generalship.

6. I want to remind you, gentlemen, of that day on which, holding the elections, you passed over many [and chose] me; for [there was] no small [...], a mass of speeches, and such cries from the orators as these: 'Safety lies in arms, and the greatest part of the arms themselves lies in the general. And he ought to be not one of just anyone, but one of those who have been tested.'

7. So-and-so praised so-and-so, but you paid no attention. Another admired another, but you did not accept him. And with a third and a fourth, I think, it was the same: those praising, those not persuaded. For of some you blamed the ancestors, of others that they had not been well brought up, of others that they had no experience of contests, of others that they were slow to find what was needed, of others that they were not able to carry out what had been decided.

8. But when someone mentioned me, everyone, gentlemen, accepted [me]; for even if it is rather vulgar to say, I shall not keep silent. The whole people burst into uproar, and was disposed like someone who has heard [the name of] the man he had long been looking for, and chose [me] with pleasure and good hopes.

So I, having taken over affairs and trying not to disappoint the expectation of those who chose me, did not consider how I might enjoy myself through my power and increase my property, but I kept on taking thought for this: that nothing at all through which the public interest might be improved should be overlooked. The soldiers know my labours, my sleepless nights, the many exercises in which I trained them, how I honoured the brave, how I corrected those who were not so, seeking opportunities for battle, seizures of positions, guard against suffering harm, plans for doing it, ambushes, schemes, exhortations, battles, the means to victory.

But thinking that the best general must not take forethought for prevailing outside while neglecting what is inside the wall, I, who even before was not ignorant of the laws, was then eager to know them better [and] to make them secure. For I knew that the city is stronger than its enemies through the laws by which it is governed, but falls into disorder when these are disturbed.
Therefore one must defeat the enemy not by driving them off, but by the laws being strong.

Now I saw that all [the laws] were beneficial and worth guarding, but especially the one that declares that a foreigner must not take part in our assemblies. Why? Because, gentlemen, it is of great weight that what has been resolved should escape notice, and the same decree, if kept hidden, is a gain to those who passed it, but if proclaimed before the deeds, is useless, and sometimes has even harmed those who resolved it.

Knowing, then, that while this law prevails there is some use even in arms, but when it is abolished battles are a fruitless business, I kept watch in the assemblies so that the gathering should be pure, of the citizens alone, for whom goodwill towards their native land is a necessity, and that none of those who might easily report to the enemy what prevailed here should be present; and I myself cast my eyes about everywhere, and so did those to whom this very task had been assigned, and they were not few. For I placed my hopes of trophies in the assemblies, and, as one might say, it was a more useful work than allies that no outsider should know our secrets. For this reason, too, it seems to me, the lawgiver summons the general, and not the other magistrates, against the foreigner, knowing that strictness in these matters will concern most the man to whom it is most advantageous that they not be violated.

13. At other times, then, foreigners yielded to our laws, and none was seen to be bolder than his fear [allowed]; but the other day, when we were sitting together, and there was great anxiety and deliberation about the gravest matters, and the herald was asking 'Who wishes to speak?', and those who had considered [the matter] were standing up, I was watching each man in service to the law, and those to whom this was assigned were going about.

Suddenly a shout and commotion: 'This foreigner is forcing his way in and learning what has been said, what has been decided, what was resolved and what was not, and, come from who knows where, he will go away knowing the city's affairs. The general sits quiet, no punishment appears, no sword anywhere.'

When such things had come to light and were being said, what should I have done? Praise the man, crown him, order [you] to regard the law as mere words, and open the assemblies to foreigners? No one will say so. What then remained? To lead him off, to confirm the law by deed. So I did what I would have broken the law by not doing, and he uttered just those things that people arrested for death usually say, which it is commonly thought right for all to disregard, and he suffered what had been laid down as the penalty for such acts.

After this, then, while you admired me for how carefully and diligently I scrutinised the assemblies and how vigorously I punished those who despised the city, there came in from somewhere the god-hated tyranny. That I was distressed at it along with you, you know. At any rate, everything that had to be said, examined, planned and done by me to stop the horrors, I think I contributed to you eagerly, as at least I persuade myself.

17. And the lawlessness has passed, and we are a democracy again, and you sacrifice and pour libations, and all except me are in good cheer; but the general is on trial, and, most absurd of all, as having helped the tyrant overthrow the laws. What then is my argument? Simple and just. You say I was an accomplice and took part in the tyranny? Very well. Then let whoever knows this appear, let him testify, let him show himself to the jurors, let him persuade those who have sworn the oath that by killing me they will not commit perjury. For this is a proper accusation. 'This man has stolen.' What is the proof? 'So-and-so testifies.' 'The defendant has committed adultery.' From what are we to be persuaded? 'From the testimony.'

Let this, this very thing, be kept for me now too. 'The general was privy to these things with the man who was going to become tyrant.' He has charged this in writing. Then call, in support of the indictment, the witnesses as well, whether free men or slaves, anyone at all whom you can call, whether of the archers, whether of the hoplites, whether of the cavalry, whether slingers, whether citizens, whether foreigners. For democracy differs from tyranny in this: there it is enough for the master to give the order, and a man must die; here, before the accused is shown to have dared deeds deserving death, it is not possible for him to be punished with death.

And you, in demanding that I die on a bare charge, think your demand reasonable? Why, if you were accusing me of outrage, or of assault, or of slander, would you not rightly be asked even then: 'In whose presence did I behave outrageously, in whose presence did I strike, who was there when I spoke ill?' But you, [charging me with] the greatest of crimes, one that surpasses everything among men (for what could be more impious than tyranny?), bringing in such an indictment and offering signs and shadows, do you think you will persuade those who are voting?

20. Of crimes, gentlemen, some have their force from the wrongdoer alone, others from the participation of many. For example, someone plotted to kill his enemy in the evening as he was leaving dinner. This he could do even alone, and he would have no need to call in accomplices for the murder, nor to announce what he will do to people he would not need. Again, a doctor destroyed so-and-so with a drug, either hating him himself or having taken a fee for the murder. This man, if tried on probabilities, would not reasonably complain, saying that someone to testify against him ought to be present. Why? Because his hands and his skill were enough for him for the crime, just as for that man who slaughtered his enemy, the sword together with his hands was enough.

And yet we see even those men shouting, 'Are we then to be ruined without witnesses?', and seeming to many to complain with good reason. But tyranny is not a thing of that kind; rather, the man who desires the thing must share his intention with many. And the accomplice, gentlemen, must be an accomplice together with many; and for the general, while being an accomplice, to escape the notice of the others that he is one is the most impossible thing of all.

For consider: when that man told me what he had decided to do and disclosed his desire, he would have told me in advance not because he thought that this in itself was to his advantage, that I should not be ignorant of anything being done, but because he was buying the assurance that no obstacle would arise for him from those posted under me, if anyone should get wind of it.

Then the general cooperating with him ought, best of all, to have discussed with his whole force the need to let so-and-so overthrow the laws, and to have taught them that the daring venture pleased me; or if not this, [to have spoken] to the taxiarchs, to the phylarchs, to the others through whom it would have been possible to hold the soldiers back at the critical moment. But if I knew, while they were ignorant and would have prevented it if they had perceived it, what more would the tyrant have gained from my partnership without that of the men under my command?

24. Why, then, have I gone through this? So that it may become clear to you, gentlemen, that, if any of this were true, the very nature of the matter would have supplied this man with many witnesses, who, even if they kept silent then, eyeing with suspicion my distinction and the honour I received from you, would now in the trial and in the abuse have attacked me, summoned by the occasion. And a general is in many ways a vexation to those who follow him, ordering them to toil, blaming those who hang back in battles, giving such men grief at the distributions.

Some of these, then, ought to have been standing by this man and testifying that the indictment is truthfully written, and, by Zeus, not a few of my own household slaves as well. For that so great an undertaking would have required many words and much time, and that every day [we] would have had either to meet in person to confer and consider, or to communicate with each other through others and to send and receive messages about the matter, is clear, I think, to all. As for those who performed these services: if he says some of them were household slaves, why does he not call them? If they were friends, why does he not use them?

Do you see those who seized power together with the tyrant, some of whom guarded his person, some garrisoned the acropolis, and some carried out whatever he ordered? If you were to ask them about one another, whether they knew each other before the tyranny, they will say that they did. For none of them would have dared without being able to look to fellow-workers.

So if I too was among the partners, and they knew this just as they knew one another, why then do you not have plenty of these [as witnesses] too, as of the others? Because, gentlemen, what has not been done cannot have witnesses. This is nothing to be wondered at for the prosecutor, but it is reasonable for me to demand it, and for you to search together with me and to compel him to produce them. For your zeal about the witnesses will save me, and will release you from the curse.

Come now, if this man had given money to some people and persuaded them to shout here that I was privy, that I was a partner, would it have sufficed for you, and would you have thought you must convict? Would you not rather have considered who the people saying this were? Whether they were hostile to me, often given to bearing false witness? Then will you, who would have distrusted witnesses who were present, believe the words of the prosecutor when they are absent?

You will then create a great abundance of those willing to play the sycophant, who now, through having to come in with witnesses or else seem to be talking nonsense, will sometimes even hold back; but if they learn that no proofs are needed and that punishment will attend accusations, some citizen will always be destroyed. For the easiest thing of all is to file an indictment and be shameless. It remains, then, for them to accuse, for you to condemn, and for none of the defendants to be acquitted.

30. Before now, someone at a loss for witnesses has turned to the disposition of the accused, and by showing that it admits the charges has seemed to have a point. But this now undoes the indictment rather than confirms it, and I am cleared of the charge on two counts: by this man's lack of witnesses, and by its being probable that I am well disposed to the city. For who does not know that those who stir up the existing constitution and desire one that is not are those who fare worse under the established one and have better hopes in change?

For example, a man cast out of a city under tyranny longs for the laws and equal freedom of speech and tries to bring these back. Again, a man for whom it is not advantageous that the laws prevail attempts to undo the laws. Who, then, are those at war with the laws? Those whose fathers were punished under them, those who owe debts to the public treasury, those against whom disfranchisement has been decreed, those whose past lives exclude them from the speaker's platform, all who, having committed many crimes, know that while the laws stand they cannot avoid paying the penalty.

32. Where then do you place me, you sycophant? What has made me an enemy of the constitution? Did I live in the prison? Was I among the debtors? Had I been stripped of free speech by vote? Had my property been confiscated? Had I been caught as a scoundrel, and did the prospect of suffering something terrible drive me to stir everything up? Or was there nothing of the kind, and was I, being upright, displaying my character among the unfeeling? Was I not praised? Was I not admired? Was I not in charge of the arms? Did I not command the forces? Was I not envied, not fortunate? Not distinguished among you? Not formidable to the enemy?

Is there, then, anyone who would deprive himself of such great goods? Yes, by Zeus, a man not in his right mind. For why would a sane man? Seeking what in place of what he had? Was I, having been thought worthy of the generalship by you, bringing a master upon the constitution in which I had become so great? And so that another might gain unjust power, did I choose to be, and to be thought, ready to do anything?

For if I myself had been going to be tyrant, would I have accepted being made tyrant instead of general, an impious thing instead of a lawful and civic one? Desiring what? To be honoured? And what is finer than honours from the people, from which compulsion is absent, which alone deserve to be called honours? A tyrant is flattered, but honoured least of all. For a man whom the one who bows before him curses, where would anyone place him among the honoured? Or so that I might live in luxury, outrage women and seize money? But I was not brought up in such habits, nor educated to love such evils.

You yourselves are witnesses to this through the generalship. For to this one man you bore witness that he was upright and of such parentage, stronger than pleasures, had practised virtue in every way, had given his leisure to the finest pursuits, and [had] everything that one would pray for for oneself and for one's children. So the generalship is a weighty token that I practised better things from childhood; but who, already holding it and honoured with the highest honours, would pass from the very rewards of virtue to being bad, and make the prizes of nobility a beginning of wickedness? No, honours are not of a nature to do this; they would rather show the base to be good than turn the better man to the other side.

So the generalship was both a prize for the life I had lived before and an encouragement to hold the more firmly to virtue. Does it seem that a man who would not have accepted being tyrant himself would ever have chosen to be attached to a tyrant in the role of a towed boat? And which was better: to lead so many brave men, or to be the slave of one corrupt man? To be crowned after victories, or to satisfy shameful pleasures for a drunken man? To receive proclamations [of honour], or to grovel before a master?

And you, who judge others so easily, if you had obtained from the people what I have, would you have committed against them the wrongs you say I committed? You did well to be disgusted at the word. Do not, then, suppose that it befits you to be just towards those who have honoured you, but that I, in the midst of my honours, betrayed those who trusted me.

38. You heard him, then, making the silliest argument of all: that the tyrant would have paid the highest price to gain my support, and that I had the power, had I wished, to help him. For who does not know that all who are at war with anyone at all would gladly buy the generals of their opponents? Are all generals therefore traitors on this account, all takers of bribes, all betrayers of their own people? It is not so: those who are wicked by nature sell themselves, but those who would gladly corrupt them do not change the minds of good men; the one side prays that they may become worse, the other stays with the better course.

And surely we must not take the wishes of those men as proof against the good. If, when I was drawn up against the enemy without reproach, someone had brought forward deserters from there and accused me of treason, saying that the deserters knew that this had often been said among their own people: that if anyone persuaded the general of their opponents to become a traitor, [their side] would gladly have borne [the cost] — if, saying this, he had demanded that I be punished, is there anyone he would have persuaded? No one is so foolish.

Will the man, then, who would not have been thought to love the enemy because they would have set great store by this, be thought to have shared in the tyranny, because it would have been a great thing for the tyrant to win me over? Why, not even a man who loves a chaste woman has, by bare desire alone, disgraced her who does not even know her lover.

So do not tell us how he would have wished to do wrong with us, but show whether we would have chosen to do wrong with him. And do not put me on trial while accusing him. For now my wickedness must not be judged by the wishes of others, but [one must judge] the general's intention itself, on its own; and since you cannot show it to be base, do not slander it with the tyrant's.

42. As to the claim that I had power, a short argument suffices. If people at once do whatever they have the power to do, then I have contributed something to the tyrant, I have been wicked, I owe a penalty: take it. But if willing does not lead the deeds, being able counts for nothing more. He who did not will it has done no wrong. So where is it just to call to account a man who merely had the ability?

It is very easy for a helmsman to wreck his own ship on the headlands. Do helmsmen then do this? No. Why? Because they do not wish to. It is easiest of all for priests to live in luxury on the offerings. Do they then commit this wrong, those who are not wicked, merely because they are able? Not in the least. It is very easy for jurors to give an unjust verdict, but because they honour justice, they cast their vote accordingly.

And why mention the rest? Would killing one's slave while he sleeps, and strangling one's son, and slaughtering oneself besides, need much labour and trouble? And what, gentlemen, is easier than this? Has each of us, then, done one thing or another, or all of them in turn? Yet that would have to be so, if being able persuaded us to act. But capacities do not create the will in a person; rather, being able everywhere serves the will.

45. And now the man who cannot call me wicked will babble about power; yet the arguments by which I clear myself of the charge are not babble but the truth of the facts. For what of the things I did after he had seized control of everything bears witness that I took pleasure in what had been dared? Did I live on the acropolis? Did I use bodyguards? Did I dine with the tyrant? Did I share in his counsel? His concerns? His secrets? His words? His deeds? Did I persuade him in some things and obey him in others? Was anyone driven from the city because of me? Stripped of his money? Deprived of his wife? Did anyone drink hemlock? Did any of those who brought down orders from above say, 'This is the tyrant's, this is the general's'? Did I hand over the hoplites to him, or any of the archers? Did I reap the fruits of the lawlessness under the tyranny?

Is anyone, then, so wretched that, having shared in the impiety of the deed, he would have shunned the partnership at the point where he could enjoy the sweetest things — as if someone who had dug through a wall with another and borne his share of the fears, and then, when he could share the furniture in safety, for which everything had been risked, did not wish to?

Why then, you poor wretch, were you doing evil to no purpose? Why did you stop the partnership at the hardships and not extend it to the profit? Do you see partners in trading ventures, gentlemen, acting like this? Has anyone, after enduring the sea and the evils of the sea and reaching harbour, gone home with hands empty of the profits, yielding them to another?

Was I, alone of men, making a tyrant on condition that I should have no share in the pleasures of the tyranny? And who would believe it? It would have made much more sense for a man who had not helped bring about the despotism to want to enjoy it once it existed, than for one who had laboured to bring it into being to shun a share at the moment of enjoyment.

As it is, by the generalship I held I was harming the tyranny, and I did not take the benefits of the tyranny in exchange for the generalship. And how is it not absurd that those who associated with the tyrant have been punished for that very thing, while the man who fled that association is not, on that account, held to be upright, but is judged to deserve the same reputation as those who dared the opposite?

50. What, then, is the proof of complicity? 'Another man,' he says, 'came to denounce the tyranny, and he a foreigner, while you kept silent.' For it was not possible, my fine friend, for one who had not perceived it beforehand to cry out. And the very failure to perceive those who were skilfully plotting evil is not the wrongdoing of those who did not know. But if this is my wrongdoing, why mine alone, by the gods? Is it fitting for me alone to care for the city, while the other citizens are released from forethought?

And why do I speak of the citizens? These speakers, who come forward, propose decrees and persuade you, who say that the safekeeping of everything lies in their voices, and who are indignant if they do not receive crowns — why are they not now on trial on the same charges? For they too are among those who did not perceive, yet they have power among you.

But I leave the orators aside too: this archon here, and the prytaneis, and the council that administers most affairs — why are they not brought up on the same charges? No, it is not wrongly that they are free of the charge, by the gods, but it is not rightly that I am under it. For how many, since cities have been inhabited, have grown more ambitious than others and attacked the laws? One could not even count them. How many were caught before carrying out their design? Not a few. Did the generals, then, see all of them before anyone else? It is not so: one man the general [detected], another the orator, another someone working in the marketplace, another a slave, another a woman, another, I think, however the chances of fortune fell out. For just as it is not those who deserve to be rich who come upon treasures, but those to whom the divinity grants them, so too it is often one of the many, rather than those in high position, who has the good luck to discover such preparations.

53. And there is perhaps some reason in it, that it is to those of no great account rather than to those in high standing that such things give a perception of themselves. For the evildoer tries to escape the notice of whoever frightens him, but towards one whom he can despise he relaxes something of his care. If he hears of the general, he shudders; if of any one of the nameless, he takes courage. So in the one case he was on his guard, while in the other he even neglected something. And so some part of what was concealed was laid bare.

Something of the same sort happens with slaves who do wrong. For those who try to pilfer their masters' property have often been informed on by those whom one would not have expected, while the steward did not notice. And, by Zeus, one of the neighbours learned of the plot before the fellow slaves did. What wonder, then, if in the public affairs of the city too something similar happens, and a man plotting against the laws, while escaping the notice of the one he thought would stop him, became plain to the one he did not suppose would care?

'A foreigner came to tell.' Naturally. For if someone plots against a city, he does not also make the preparations by which he expects to prevail in that very city. That would be the act of a man wishing to die, not of one desiring tyranny. For who would not have been suspicious, seeing a crowd of men being gathered, a mass of weapons being made ready, drinking parties, meetings, men running about, men flattering, in short everything needed by those who mean to overpower the people?

For this reason they plot against the laws [here], but prepare elsewhere what is needed for the deed; and they escape the notice of those whose masters they desire to become, but become plain to those from among whom they set out. Do not, then, let what usually happens by the very nature of the thing count against the generals.

57. 'And you slaughtered the foreigner,' he says, 'when he was bringing us some secret.' Add that the law commanded this. And ask these men which side creates tyranny: those who think they must uphold the laws you have, or those who put on trial the men who uphold them? Could anything be more novel than this? The indictment says that I assisted a tyranny, but the proof is that I obeyed the laws. And they call the same man both an ally of a tyrant and a guardian of the laws. Then I would rightly be on trial, then I would justly be hated, if, knowing the law and seeing the foreigner, I had put the foreigner's voice ahead of the law.

And in general, what need is there to write laws, if, when the matters arrive for which they were laid down, we shall lightly overstep them? And how is it not absurd that in the same courts some are punished as having disregarded the laws, and others as having followed the laws? Did he say he was bringing some secret? I admit it. And did I pay no attention? I admit it.

For first my respect for the law, and then my anger at the sight — that a foreigner was learning your affairs in your midst — drew me to punish him rather than attend to his words. Then, by the gods, a suspicion of this sort also came over me: 'This man has come with an enemy's intent and ran the risk in order to depart knowing the city's affairs, and now that he is caught he is fabricating what most do.' And what is that? The man who knows clearly that he will die fabricates stories so as to stave off the present danger, and throws into confusion those who have caught him with false charges against themselves.

So, snatched from their midst, those who are hostile to certain people bind, rack, torture [them], and apply every kind of evil from which they hope factions will spring up, and all that factions bring. For they think that in public uproar either safety will come or a slower end. And somehow dragging down along with them those outside the charge gives a certain pleasure to those who are justly about to perish.

I thought that foreigner too was one of these, and I swiftly used the care for the city given by the laws, lest some false word, falling among us, should overturn everything. If I judged wrongly, I erred; I did not do wrong. There is, I think, a great difference between supposing wrongly and loving a tyrant; and a loyal general is surely not the same as a prophet. The fear I felt, then, came from loyalty, but to be ignorant of nothing that was to come would have needed another art.

62. Moreover, that man himself gave grounds for suspicion, who, passing over me and the prytaneis and the other magistrates, in breach of the law watched the assembly and listened to what was said and ratified. What would one who was informing, and not scheming, have done? Come to the general's headquarters, said that he wished to meet the general, met him alone, talked with him, told the story, explained how the evil arose, where it was heading, who the tyrant was, who his accomplices, and not, before benefiting the people, harm it by contempt for the laws, nor, while claiming to care for the laws, begin his good service by breaking the law, which he surely knew was in force — unless, by Zeus, being a foreigner, he was ignorant of the constitution he was so concerned for.

'But he came when they were already assembled.' Let him have waited a little and held back. Let him approach the magistrates. For surely he was not going to shout the secret out into the assembly. That would have been the act not of one handing the quarry over to us properly, nor of one acting so that the evil might be stopped, but so that we might at once be in turmoil.

You too took this to heart, and thought the same as I about the foreigner: seeing him led off, when it was in your power to intervene and order him not to be killed, you let it happen, you permitted it; by not stopping the slaughter you approved the killing; by not blaming the man leading him you judged that the man led ought to suffer this. If you had wished to save him, what would have stood in the way? Would it not have been enough to say two words, just this: 'Let the man go'? For the general is certainly not stronger than the whole people. By letting him kill, then, you acknowledged, as far as you were concerned, that the killing was not wrong.

65. Do not, then, if it pleased everyone, let me alone be prosecuted for it — I whose disposition, apart from the times before the tyranny and my deeds during it, is shown to be democratic by what I evidently did once it had been overthrown. For I did not go off into exile, which is what a man long complicit would have done, nor did I fear being tried if I stayed. I did not consider withdrawing any safety.

And yet, when men were already attacking the tyrant and regaining their freedom, and affairs were seething, it would have been very easy to take my wife and children, go elsewhere, and live beyond your laws in complete security. But for me, who had done you no wrong, nothing was sweeter than my fatherland. So I stayed, confident, with no fear driving me out.

Do not, then, gentlemen, consider a lawful killing done along with you, in ignorance of the future, a sign of wickedness rather than my not being disturbed by the overthrow of the tyrant a token of the general's justice; and when there are so many things that dissolve the charge — zeal in my generalship, hatred towards enemies, the care for the laws that I took on your behalf, the very fact that I remained among you in the change of affairs — do not give more weight to the cleverness of the accusers than to the truth of the deeds.

A foul breed, gentlemen, the breed of sycophants, is nourished in cities against the established laws, against decent men, against sworn jurors. For they tear apart those who do no wrong, and in doing so they destroy the laws, and those who sit bound by their oaths they inflict the greatest damage on along with the defendants. For the one perish, while the others live under a curse and pass the harm on to their children.

Just as, then, we drive back enemies together with arms, so the shamelessness and violence of the sycophants must be restrained by those who judge on each occasion. Because of them, doing no wrong carries the same dangers as villainy, and the most decent man and the most foul are brought alike under the votes. And indeed more of the good perish than of the worse. For the latter, along with their crimes, take thought for what they will say, while the former, trusting in the lives they have lived, are handed over unprepared to those who practise speaking.

Make this practice of theirs vain, gentlemen, their cleverness feeble and their shamelessness fruitless. For as it is, having abandoned the other occupations by which the best of the citizens live, they reap the courts, sharpening their tongues instead of swords. Someone gave [them money] out of fear: 'excellent, decent, worthy of praise.' Someone, doing no wrong, refused to pay anything out: 'wicked, tyrannical, he has done every wrong.'

Let each of the jurors, then, believe that he will soon be one of the defendants, and let him leave his own vote about others as an example to those who will later judge him, teaching them not to side with these wild beasts who are persuading you to hand over to the executioner the man whom you lately praised and set over the whole state. And what could be more shameful for a city than when its generals themselves, whose passion is to die under arms, depart [this life] by the vote of jurors? Do you not know that, besides its being unjust to kill the blameless, it also leads the enemy to despise your generals, as men not brought to this rank by merit?

Now, then, the name of tyranny, turned up and down by the accusers, has roused you; but you must bear in mind that some, having already condemned a defendant to death, have afterwards taken themselves to task, when there was no longer any remedy for the harm, and only one thing remained, to blame themselves. May you not suffer that now. For indeed, if you were only going to lose a general, it would perhaps be no great matter; but as it is, gentlemen, the question before you concerns the laws.

How is it that I am on trial for having kept a law, the law which, by keeping your deliberations secret, enables [you] to overcome the enemy? If, then, I am punished for this vigilance, who will not abolish the sacred laws, the military laws, those on traitors, those on chastity, those on temple-robbers and tomb-breakers? I pass over the rest, gentlemen.

What foreigner will any longer fear the assemblies, who will not come? Who will not dare? Who will not slip in and sit there gathering up the measures that carry the day among you, for those who seek their own advantage? And which of your decrees will not be carried out to every part of land and sea? What secret any longer, by Zeus, will make the city stronger than its enemies, when they know with what plans we are going out to fight against them?

So those sending spies here will be many, those serving them in this not few, and the one punishing those who are caught, nobody. Or tell me, what general, looking closely at my punishment, whoever he may be, will not know this: that it is very easy for the one caught to say that he came on the city's behalf, while the one who upholds the law will face the same things that I face, an accuser and an indictment? Who, then, is so foolish as to wish to be at the mercy of those whom he is trying to benefit?

What I said, then, to my friends, when they urged me to beg myself off by means of my children's tears, I will say to you as well. I have children, gentlemen, being brought up according to your laws and always hearing this from me: to live as those [laws] command. I forbade anyone to bring them to the platform. For may no general be saved among you through pity for his children, or a weeping wife, or a mother in tears, or the grey hair of a weeping father, or friends standing by. Let each man be acquitted or punished on the basis of what he has done; if a man is childless but just, let him go away unharmed, and if he is the father of many but wicked, let him die.

To what, then, would I ask you to look instead of my children? To the good discipline of the soldiers, the expeditions, the battles, the stratagems, the deeds. Send secretly to the enemy. Ask whether I am hated among them, and consider that it belongs to the same spirit to hold no converse about the city with its enemies, whether those outside it or those within.

Why so gloomy and downcast, taxiarchs, captains and soldiers? Does some memory come over you of those infantry battles and of all the victories we won with cavalry, and do you long for your leader? Do you recall the anxieties and deliberations and grief we lived with while the tyranny pressed upon us, the sacrifices at which we prayed, the processions in which we marched, the mysteries we shared, the toils we endured, the hopes we hoped?

But bear it, men, bear the present trial. There is no city that is free of the sycophant. Even if I die by the vote, bear this too. Consider that I have fallen to an enemy's missile. Another general will take you over, perhaps no better in other respects, but more fortunate.

I go away with some consolation for my end. I have seen the city free, I have seen the laws strong, I have seen the people assembling. I see trials held by the water-clock. Leaving my children in this security, I depart. By one thing only am I troubled: that through fear some neglect of the laws may arise among the generals, and they may judge it more expedient to gratify this man than to be on the side of justice.

But, you successors to my post, may you never be party to unjust judgements; consider no indictment more fearful than becoming bad men with regard to the laws, and do not throw open the assemblies to foreigners, but keep the city safe above all by these two things: strength in arms and keeping the established laws.
